Senator Feingold now serves as the president of the American Constitution Society, which is a progressive legal organization that advocates for the rule of law, democratic legitimacy and equality for all. Senator Feingold, thank you for joining us.

So, Senator Feingold, can you tell us again how during your Senate career you identified that the financing of campaigns was becoming a threat to democracy and how you formed the bipartisan relationship with Senator John McCain to sort of address the threat of big money in politics?

Well, you know, that covers a lot of time because, you know, when I graduated from law school, I came back to Wisconsin where I wanted to practice law. But I had this political bug ever since a guy named John F. Kennedy was elected president when I was seven years old. And much to the consternation of some of my family members, I wanted to run for office. But even back then in 1982, people would say, where are you going to get the money? On the other hand, it wasn't that much money then. We had a successful public financing system in Wisconsin then. So when I ran for the state Senate as a 29-year-old, The deal was if you could raise $17,000 from contributions of $100 or less, the state would give you $17,000. And that was basically enough in those days for a state Senate campaign. Now, I only won by 31 votes out of 47,000 against an 83-year-old incumbent. But it wasn't a Republican district. And I can't say, and I think anyone would say that money was the key. So I had a successful 10 years in the Wisconsin State Senate from 1983 to 1993. But I started thinking about running for the US Senate. And I was sort of taken as not a serious candidate. because I didn't have a lot of money, either personally or access to it. And so that was the argument all along. And when I ran in 1992 for the US Senate, just as Paul Wellstone did in Minnesota in 1990, we basically ran as underdog saying, look, we don't have millions of dollars, because at that time the problem was that millionaires would come in and spend a fortune at happening Wisconsin and sort of buy Senate seats. So that's kind of where it was at when I was lucky enough to use the underdog argument to flip the table. And I was able to get in the US Senate, the youngest member of the US Senate at age 39. And within just a couple of years, of course, I was eager to see national campaign fighting. But the Democrats were in control. And I would say I was like, you know, maybe the 10th guy on campaign fighting. There were people already working out ahead of me. People with names like Biden and Kerry. So I just was glad to be in the room, but we lost the majority. And you may remember in 1994, they called it the Republican tsunami. They came in and I figured not only was I the least senior member of the entire Senate in terms of seniority. But the last thing I expected was to get a call at that point, right as the Republicans took over, from Republican Senator John McCain of Arizona. But he called me right after the election in 94 and said, hey, I want to work on reform issues with you. You seem to be a reformer. I want to be a reformer. Let's work together on something. And so I said, what do you have in mind? He said, well, you know, this thing where people become senators and go to a case street and make all kinds of money. revolving door and I said, well, let's get rid of gifts from members of Congress. I saw this stuff coming to my office, guns and Christmas trees and golf clubs and everything. And we said, let's get rid of that. So McCain and I did that first. It wasn't until later in 1995 that we finally came together and said, let's do the big one, but let's do campaign finance. And the reason was that we had gone not just from big expensive campaign to the advent of something called soft money, unlimited dark money contributions that were taking the scandal of campaign finance to a whole new level. So that is condensed 20 years into a couple of minutes. I hope it wasn't too long.

turn_text: And kind of getting to the partisanship or bipartisan legislation you passed with Senator McCain, can you tell us a bit more about the other parts of what was in the legislation and how effective it was in the early years and kind of we'll get to Citizens United next, of course.

Well, it was really an exciting process. It took seven or eight years. John and I would hold a news conference at the end of every year when we'd get beat. Of course, we needed 60 votes to get this. But at first, we only had three people. It was just me and him and Senator Fred Thompson, the late Senator from Tennessee, the actor. who said that when things were going well, we called it just McCain Feingold, but when things weren't going well, we called it McCain Feingold, Thompson, one of the jokes. But with very slow process, we got Susan Collins to join us when she came in 1996, because Maine had just passed public financing, and it was becoming more and more of an issue as there were scandals in the Clinton campaign. I don't know if you remember, there was a $400,000 contribution from an Indonesian gardener that had been just sort of funneled through other sources. And so John and I decided this had to be bipartisan. You'd never get 60 votes if you couldn't do that, obviously. And so we decided it would be if you, if one of us lined it up, somebody from our party, you had to get somebody from the other guy's party to come into the group, the core group. So I call it the animals go two by two. And we ended up having 10 of the most distinguished members of the Senate, people like Carl Levin and Joe Lieberman and many others become part of our group and we were able to sort of control the process. The main provisions were originally to try to just limit the amount of cost if somebody limited how much they spent in a campaign. that they could get reduced costs on their television time. But we weren't able to get enough people to sign on to that because the broadcaster is so powerful. We decided in the end that simply banning these unlimited contributions going through the political parties was the most important thing. There were other provisions added later that had to do with these phony issue ads. that was important as well, but not as important. That's what was struck down by the Supreme Court. But the fundamental process of parties being able to raise unlimited money is still the law of the land. But it doesn't do a lot when you have something like Citizens United go around it and striking down the ban on corporate contribution. which is what was the 1907 law. And that's the thing that sort of undid the system. But we were able to gradually pick up support. And we passed the McCain Feingold bill in April of 2001. Many people thought that when 9-11 occurred that that was it, nobody would focus on this, but we got it through the house. And we got it signed by George Bush, who didn't want to sign it, but he signed it. And so as I remind people, this bill, was passed by a Republican Senate, a Republican House, a Republican president, and a Supreme Court, approved by a Supreme Court on a five-to-four vote that was a majority Republican appointee. So it really was bipartisan.
